To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the hydrolysis kinetics of organophosphate (OP) flame retardants in natural waters is controlled by the pH of the water and the mineralogy of the sediments.

the hydrolysis rate constants of OPFRs in the presence of minerals are much faster than in homogeneous solution, and the hydrolysis half lives are reduced to days, which is important for environmental fate.
organophosphate flame-retardants are rapidly hydrolyzed by metal oxide minerals, and that mineral catalyze hydrolysis could be a major fate-controlling sink in natural environments.

the environmental fate of organophosphate esters (OPEs) and organophosphate ester flame retardants (OPEFRs), a group of chemicals with increasing use in recent years.
the fate and behavior of emerging contaminants in aquatic and terrestrial environments.
the fate and transport of organophosphate esters (OPEs) in the environment, and in particular with the degradation of OPEs in soil and aquatic environments.

mineral catalyze hydrolysis is a significant fate controlling sink of OPFRs in natural environments.
